cards.front: Is driving above the posted limit in a highway work zone lawful?
cards.back: Driving faster than the posted speed limit inside a highway work zone is unlawful.

cards.front: Where does a highway work zone begin and end?
cards.back: A highway work zone runs from the first sign marking where the zone begins to the last sign marking where it ends.

cards.front: When does an extra speeding penalty apply in a work zone?
cards.back: If a sign at the start of a work zone lists a speeding penalty, that penalty is added on top of any other penalty for the speeding conviction.

cards.front: How do the work zone boundaries relate to the extra penalty?
cards.back: A work zone begins at the first work zone sign and ends at the last one, and an extra speeding penalty applies only when a sign at the start lists it.
cards.memory_hook: zone by signs, penalty if posted

cards.front: What are orange signs with black lettering used for?
cards.back: Orange signs with black lettering are used only to identify work zones, both on the approach and inside the zone.

cards.front: What does a Flagger sign tell you?
cards.back: A Flagger sign means a worker in an orange vest ahead is directing traffic with a STOP and SLOW paddle, so stay alert and be ready to stop.

cards.front: When should you act on a black-on-orange advance sign?
cards.back: Black-on-orange advance signs may tell you to act, such as moving to another lane, and they give that message early enough that you should not wait until the last moment.

cards.front: What is a leading cause of rear-end collisions in work zones?
cards.back: In work zones, going slower than the traffic around you is a leading cause of rear-end collisions, because confined lanes may leave no escape route.

cards.front: Which devices guide drivers through a work zone?
cards.back: Barricades, cones, drums and flaggers are the traffic control devices used to guide drivers safely through a work zone.

cards.front: When does North Carolina law require headlights?
cards.back: North Carolina law requires headlights from sunset to sunrise and whenever you cannot see more than four hundred feet ahead.
cards.memory_hook: sunset to sunrise, or low visibility

cards.front: What are the two triggers that require headlights?
cards.back: Headlights are required from sunset to sunrise and also whenever visibility drops to four hundred feet or less, even in daytime.

cards.front: When must you turn on headlights because of your wipers?
cards.back: North Carolina requires every driver to turn on headlights whenever the windshield wipers are in use because of bad weather.

cards.front: When should you use low beams and high beams at night?
cards.back: At night use low beams in the city, and on the open road use high beams except when approaching or following another vehicle.

cards.front: Why is driving at night riskier?
cards.back: Night driving is riskier because visibility is lower, more impaired and tired drivers are out, and oncoming headlights can blind you.

cards.front: What should you do if an oncoming driver keeps high beams on?
cards.back: If an oncoming driver keeps high beams on, blink your high beams once as a reminder; if they still do not dim, stay on low beam.

cards.front: If an oncoming driver will not dim, should you switch to high beams?
cards.back: Flash your high beams once to remind an oncoming driver to dim, but if they do not, keep your own lights on low rather than switching to high beams.

cards.front: How should you avoid oncoming headlight glare at night?
cards.back: To avoid headlight glare at night, slow down and look slightly toward the right edge of the road instead of into oncoming lights.

cards.front: How fast is too fast at night?
cards.back: Never drive so fast at night that you could not stop within the stretch of road you can actually see.

cards.front: What lights should you use when parked beside a highway at night?
cards.back: When parked on or beside a highway at night, turn on the emergency flashers and switch off the headlights so they do not blind oncoming drivers.

cards.front: What should you do about sun glare?
cards.back: For sun glare, lower the visor and wear sunglasses; if that is not enough, pull off to the roadside until you can drive safely.

cards.front: What must you use in rain, and how should your speed change?
cards.back: In rain you must use your headlights and wipers, and you should drive more slowly than normal.

cards.front: How much longer can stopping take on slippery pavement, and what following gap should you allow?
cards.back: Stopping on slippery pavement can take from two to ten times as far as on dry pavement, so allow at least double the usual following distance.

cards.front: How does the wet-road stopping multiplier compare with the following-distance rule?
cards.back: Wet pavement can stretch stopping distance from two to ten times, which is why the following gap should be at least doubled.

cards.front: When are roads slickest during rain, and why?
cards.back: Roads are slickest in the first ten to fifteen minutes of rain, when water mixes with oil, dirt, dust and rubber on the surface.

cards.front: How much slower should you drive on wet pavement?
cards.back: On wet pavement drive at least five to ten miles per hour slower than you would on dry pavement.
cards.memory_hook: wet road, five to ten slower

cards.front: When should you avoid cruise control?
cards.back: Never use cruise control during or after rain, because the time spent switching it off in a hydroplane could cost you control.

cards.front: Is cruise control fine once the rain has stopped?
cards.back: Cruise control stays off not only while it rains but also after the rain, since releasing it during a hydroplane costs time you may not have.

cards.front: What is hydroplaning, and how early can it start?
cards.back: Hydroplaning happens when a thin layer of water lifts the tires off the road, and it can begin at speeds as low as thirty miles per hour in water just over one or eight inch deep.

cards.front: What should you do if your car hydroplanes?
cards.back: If you hydroplane, lift your foot off the gas, do not brake, keep the wheel straight and let the car slow until the tires grip again.

cards.front: What speed can start hydroplaning, and what is the response?
cards.back: Hydroplaning can start at about thirty miles per hour in water just over one or eight inch deep, and the response is to ease off the gas without braking.

cards.front: How do tires affect hydroplaning risk?
cards.back: Deep, open tire tread helps prevent hydroplaning, while worn or under-inflated tires raise the risk; for skid handling, tire pressure on the high side of the maker's range is better.

cards.front: What are signs of standing water on the road?
cards.back: Signs of standing water include reflections on the surface, dimples from raindrops, a slushing tire sound and a loose feel in the steering.

cards.front: How long after rain can puddles cause hydroplaning?
cards.back: Puddles left by rain can cause hydroplaning for hours or even days after the rain stops.

cards.front: What share of North Carolina tropical-weather deaths since nineteen seventy came from inland flooding?
cards.back: Since one thousand nine hundred seventy, inland flooding has caused eighty-five percent of tropical-weather deaths in North Carolina, and half of those involved people driving onto roads known to be flooded.

cards.front: Should you drive through standing water on a road?
cards.back: Never drive through standing water on a road, since it may be deeper than it looks and part of the road may be washed out.

cards.front: How much fast-moving water can sweep a car off the road, and how much can float it?
cards.back: About six inches of fast-moving water can sweep a car off the road, and about twelve inches can float it or roll it over.

cards.front: How do the sweeping depth and the floating depth differ?
cards.back: About six inches of fast water can sweep a car off the road, while about twelve inches can float or overturn it.

cards.front: What should you do if fog is so thick you can barely see?
cards.back: If fog is so thick you can barely see, pull well off the road, stop, secure the car, turn on the flashers, exit on the passenger side and stay away from the road.

cards.front: If you must drive in fog, which lights and habits help?
cards.back: If you must drive in fog, use low beams, slow down, watch for the taillights ahead and keep an eye on vehicles behind you.

cards.front: How does handling thick fog differ from driving in lighter fog?
cards.back: In thick fog you pull far off and exit on the passenger side, while in drivable fog you use low beams and watch for the taillights ahead.

cards.front: Which road spots are often the first to freeze?
cards.back: Bridges, overpasses and shady spots are often the first places to freeze as temperatures fall.

cards.front: How much should you slow down on packed snow and on ice?
cards.back: In a snowstorm, slow down and use wipers and low beams; cut speed by more than half on packed snow and slow to a crawl on ice.

cards.front: How should you start moving on snow or ice?
cards.back: On snow or ice, speed up gently, test your steering and braking feel, and in a manual car start in second gear or higher with a slow clutch release.

cards.front: How much stopping distance should you allow on snow or ice, and how should you stop?
cards.back: Allow at least three times the normal stopping distance on snow or ice, and when stopping keep off the brake so the engine slows the car.

cards.front: On snow or ice, should you stop with the brake pedal or the engine?
cards.back: On snow or ice allow at least three times the normal stopping distance, and to stop you lift off the brake and let the engine do the slowing.

cards.front: Can chains and snow tires make quick moves safe on ice?
cards.back: Chains and snow tires can still slide on ice and packed snow, so you cannot start, stop or steer quickly in those conditions.

cards.front: How can you reduce wildlife collisions?
cards.back: Wildlife collisions can be reduced by slowing down and scanning road edges, especially at dawn, dusk and into the night.

cards.front: Why does a slower speed matter in a deer strike?
cards.back: Slower speed improves survival for both deer and driver: a deer hit at thirty-five miles per hour is far less likely to be fatal than one hit at fifty-five miles per hour or more.

cards.front: When are animals most active?
cards.back: Animals are most active at dawn, at dusk and in the first few hours after dark, and spring and fall migrations call for extra caution.

cards.front: When should you use high beams where animals may be?
cards.back: Use high beams only when there is no oncoming traffic and no animal right ahead, since bright lights can freeze some animals in place.

cards.front: Why avoid high beams when an animal is directly ahead?
cards.back: Use high beams only with no oncoming traffic and no animal directly ahead, because bright beams can freeze some animals in the road.

cards.front: After you see one deer, what should you expect?
cards.back: Many animals such as deer travel in groups, so after seeing one, expect others to follow close behind.

cards.front: What should you do when an animal is in the roadway?
cards.back: When an animal is in the roadway, hold your lane and brake firmly to stop if you can; a short honk of the horn is also an option.

recap_hooks.text: A work zone runs from the first sign to the last, and speeding there is unlawful.
Orange signs mark work zones; act early on their messages.
Headlights from sunset to sunrise, below four hundred feet of visibility, and whenever wipers are on.
Blink once to remind a driver to dim, then stay on low beams.
Slippery roads can take two to ten times as far to stop, so double the gap.
No cruise control during or after rain.
Hydroplaning can start at thirty miles per hour.
If you hydroplane, ease off the gas, do not brake, and keep the wheel straight.
Six inches of fast water can sweep a car away, and twelve can float it.
In thick fog, pull far off and exit on the passenger side.
Bridges, overpasses and shade freeze first.
On snow or ice, allow three times the stopping distance and let the engine slow you.
Slow down and scan the edges at dawn, dusk and after dark.
Where there is one deer, expect more.
